summary.text: The exponential function is the unique real function that maps zero to one and has a derivative everywhere equal to its value.
Its argument works as an exponent on the constant e ≈ 2.718, and the function converts sums to products: exp (x + y) = exp x⋅exp y.
Its inverse function, the natural logarithm, converts products to sums: ln (x⋅y) = ln x + ln y.

facts.label: The base
facts.value: e ≈ 2.718, raised to the power x

facts.label: Inverse function
facts.value: The natural logarithm, written ln or log

facts.label: Graph shape
facts.value: Upward-sloping, and always above the x-axis

facts.label: Slope rule
facts.value: The tangent's slope at each point equals its height there

facts.label: General form
facts.value: Functions of the form f(x) = abˣ are also called exponential

items.prompt: A curve is drawn so that, at every point, the slope of its tangent is exactly as large as its height above the x-axis. Which graph is it?
items.explain: For y = eˣ the slope of the tangent at each point equals its height (its y-coordinate) at that point.

items.prompt: You know the values of exp 2 and exp 3 and want exp 5. What do you do with them?
items.explain: The exponential function converts sums to products: exp (x + y) = exp x⋅exp y, and 5 = 2 + 3.

items.prompt: You know the natural logarithms of 4 and of 5 and need the natural logarithm of 20. What do you do?
items.explain: The natural logarithm converts products to sums: ln (x⋅y) = ln x + ln y, and 20 = 4⋅5.

items.prompt: A savings pile grows so that its speed of growth at any moment is proportional to how much is already in it. What kind of function describes this?

options.label: A function that adds the same amount each step
An exponential function, such as f(x) = abˣ
A function that equals its own square
A function that stays below the x-axis

items.explain: Exponential functions grow or decay so that the rate of change is proportional to the current value of f(x).

items.prompt: Far to the left on the graph of y = eˣ, where x is a large negative number, what does the curve do?

options.label: Gets arbitrarily close to the x-axis
Crosses the x-axis and goes negative
Levels off at a height of 1

items.explain: The graph always lies above the x-axis but becomes arbitrarily close to it for large negative x, so the x-axis is a horizontal asymptote.

items.prompt: A lab measures a quantity that follows f(x) = abˣ. The lab switches to a different measurement unit. Which constant changes?
items.explain: A change of measurement unit changes the value of a, which is why it makes no sense to insist that a = 1.

beats.title: A curve that feeds itself
beats.hook: Some curves climb at a speed that depends on how high they already are.

beats.prompt: A quantity follows f(x) = abˣ, so its rate of change is proportional to its current value. If the value doubles, what happens to the rate?
beats.explain: Proportional means the rate moves in step with the value, so a doubled value gives a doubled rate.

choices.label: It stays the same
choices.feedback: It would only stay put if the rate ignored the current value, but here the rate is tied to it.

choices.label: It is cut in half
choices.feedback: The rate grows with the value rather than shrinking against it.

beats.prompt: match each expression to its partner
beats.explain: The exponential turns sums into products, the natural logarithm turns products into sums, and the functional equation gives the reciprocal rules.

beats.prompt: On the graph of y = eˣ you stand at a point whose height is 5. How steep is the tangent there?
beats.explain: The slope of the tangent at each point is equal to the height at that point.

choices.label: Slope 0.5
choices.feedback: Nothing in the rule shrinks the slope below the height.

choices.label: Slope 1
choices.feedback: A slope of 1 appears at x = 0, not at every point; the slope changes along the curve.

beats.prompt: one step in this reasoning is wrong; which?

steps.text: The exponential function satisfies e⁰ = 1, so it starts above zero.
If eˣ < 0 for some x, the function would have to hit zero between 0 and x.
But eˣ ≠ 0 for every x, so eˣ > 0 for every real number x.
Since eˣ equals its derivative and is positive, it is monotonically decreasing.

beats.explain: A function that is positive and equals its derivative has a positive slope everywhere, so it is monotonically increasing, not decreasing.

beats.idea: An exponential function changes at a rate proportional to its current value, and its inverse, the natural logarithm, turns products into sums.

paragraphs.heading: The exponential function
paragraphs.text: The exponential function is the one real function that sends zero to one and whose derivative is equal to its own value everywhere. It is written eˣ, or exp x when the input is a long expression. The name comes from treating the input x as an exponent on a fixed number, e ≈ 2.718, which is called the base.

paragraphs.heading: Turning sums into products
paragraphs.text: Its key rule turns addition into multiplication: exp (x + y) = exp x⋅exp y. It also sends 0, the identity for addition, to 1, the identity for multiplication. Running the function backwards gives its inverse, the natural logarithm, written ln or log. The logarithm does the opposite job and turns products into sums: ln (x⋅y) = ln x + ln y.

paragraphs.heading: The shape of the graph
paragraphs.text: The graph of y = eˣ slopes upward, and it rises faster than any power of x. It always stays above the x-axis, since eˣ > 0 for every real number x. For large negative x it comes as close to the axis as you like, so the x-axis is a horizontal asymptote. The rule that the function equals its own derivative has a picture too: at every point, the slope of the tangent to the graph equals the height of the graph there.

paragraphs.heading: Other bases
paragraphs.text: Fixing some other base b and letting the exponent vary gives functions of the form f(x) = bˣ, and these are also called exponential functions. For a positive base b, one has b = exp (ln b), and this lets you define bˣ = exp (xln b) for every real number x. In applications the name stretches further, to functions of the form f(x) = abˣ. These grow or decay exponentially: the rate at which f(x) changes as x increases is proportional to the current value of f(x).

paragraphs.heading: A test for exponential behaviour
paragraphs.text: There is a simple check for whether measured values follow an exponential function. For any fixed step d, the ratio f(x + d)/f(x) must come out the same whatever x you start from. This matters in the empirical sciences, because it allows a direct experimental test. The constant a in abˣ has a practical role as well: switching the unit of measurement changes a, so it makes no sense to insist that a = 1.

paragraphs.heading: Beyond real numbers
paragraphs.text: The function can also accept complex numbers as inputs. Doing so ties together multiplying complex numbers, rotating in the complex plane, and trigonometry. Euler's formula, e^iθ = cos θ + isin θ, sums up these ties in one line. The idea stretches further still, to inputs such as matrices.
